newsitem.title: IRAN: Aid starts flowing to Iran after killer quake.
newsitem.headline: Aid starts flowing to Iran after killer quake.

text.p: International aid started flowing to Iran as relief agencies and governments on Monday responded to an Iranian appeal for assistance after a strong earthquake killed about 2,400 people and made 50,000 homeless.

Several countries made pledges or said they had sent aid, including the United States, which Iran's Islamic government sees as its arch-enemy, and European Union states involved in a diplomatic row with Tehran.

The United States said it was contributing $100,000 through the International Committee of the Red Cross to help the victims of the quake which left 6,000 people injured and flattened some 200 villages in a remote mountainous area in eastern Iran.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington had had disputes with the Iranian government for many years, "but we don't have any arguments with the people of Iran. The people of Iran obviously are in need of support".
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel pledged 500,000 marks ($290,000) in relief, saying Germany would not let a row get in the way of helping the country's earthquake victims.
He was referring to the dispute sparked by a Berlin court's verdict that said Iran's leaders had ordered political killings in Germany. Tehran has denied the accusations.
France said it was sending a 30-strong rescue squad backed by sniffer dogs and a first French plane carrying 39 tonnes of emergency equipment and medicine had already landed in Iran.

Italy said it was sending 36 tonnes of medicines and other aid, worth around 500 million lire ($300,000), which would be flown to Tehran in the next few days. Rome said it was also donating $30,000 through to the World Health Organisation.
United Nations agencies pledged $360,000 in aid, beginning with a $50,000 cash grant, a U.N. spokesman said in New York.

A U.N. official said earlier in Tehran rescue and relief work was going well but three strong quakes that rocked Iran in the past four months had put a huge strain on its emergency supplies and sparked an urgent need for international help.
Iran has put initial estimates of the extent of damage in the region at 300 billion rials ($100 million) after the Saturday quake which measured 7.1 on the richter scale.
Iran's Arab neighbours Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates said they were sending aid. So did Egypt.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE said they were sending two planeloads each of food, medicine, blankets and tents.
The Saudi-based Organisation of the Islamic Conference, appealed to its 52 member states to extend assistance to Iran.
Turkey said it would send two planeloads of emergency aid.

Quake-prone Iran, accustomed to dealing with natural disasters, on Sunday appealed through the United Nations for international aid. A Tehran-based U.N official said a detailed list of Iran's needs was being prepared.
Officials of the World Food Programme (WFP) were in villages near the quake's epicentre on Monday to assess the situation.
A WFP official told Reuters in the village of Baydokht the U.N. agency had sent a representative from its Rome headquarters and an Iran-based staff member to the quake-stricken area.
Iran asked for food, medicine, tents, clothing, water tanks, cookers, ambulances and four-wheel drive vehicles to use in relief work in the mountainous area near the Afghan border.
